title: Search Tree From Preorder Listing
statement:
A binary search tree with distinct values was walked in preorder: visit a node, then its whole left subtree, then its whole right subtree. You get the list of values in that order, preorder.

Rebuild the tree and return its root. In a binary search tree every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node and every value in its right subtree is larger. There is exactly one such tree for a given preorder listing.

examples.why: 6 is the root. 3, 1, 4 are smaller than 6, so they form the left subtree; 9, 12 form the right one. Note that 9 hangs off the root, not off 4, the node just before it.
Each value is smaller than everything so far, so the tree is a chain of left children.
7 is the root's right child, 5 is 7's left child, and 6 is between 5 and 7, so it is 5's right child.

constraints: All values are distinct and form a valid preorder of a binary search tree
hints: The first value is the root. Which of the following values belong to its left subtree, and where does the right subtree begin?
Every value smaller than the root comes before every larger one. Splitting at the first larger value and recursing on both parts works, but searches for the split every time.

Recurse with an upper bound instead: build a node from the next value only if it is below the bound; its left child gets the node's value as bound, its right child inherits the parent's bound. One shared index moves through the list once.

explain.intuition:
In preorder, a subtree is always a contiguous stretch of the list, starting with its root. For the root, its left subtree is the stretch of values smaller than it and its right subtree is everything after. So you can split and recurse, but finding each split costs a scan.

The faster way reads the list once, left to right, and lets bounds decide where each value goes. A call build(bound) builds the subtree that may only contain values below bound. If the next value is not below the bound, that subtree is empty and the value belongs to some ancestor's right side. Otherwise take the value as a node, build its left side with bound = the node's value, then its right side with the same bound the node had. Each value is consumed exactly once.
steps: build(bound): if i is past the end or preorder[i] > bound, return null.
Otherwise create a node with preorder[i] and advance i.
Set node.left = build(node.val), then node.right = build(bound), and return the node.
pitfalls: Attaching each larger value as the right child of the previous node. In [6, 3, 1, 4, 9] the 9 belongs to the root, not to 4.
Building the right subtree with the node's own value as bound. The right side may hold values up to the parent's bound, not up to the node.
Using a separate index per recursive call. The index must be shared so that each value is used once.

solutions.title: Insert values one by one
solutions.idea: Inserting the values into an empty search tree in preorder rebuilds exactly the original tree, since every parent is inserted before its children.
solutions.time: O(n · h), O(n²) for a chain

solutions.title: One pass with an upper bound
solutions.idea: A shared index walks the list once; each call only accepts values below its bound, so every value lands under the right ancestor.

solutions.title: Monotonic stack
solutions.idea: Keep the path of nodes still waiting for a right child, with decreasing values. A larger value pops every smaller node; the last one popped is its parent.

followups: You get the postorder listing instead. Which way do you read it, and which bound changes?
The tree is an ordinary binary tree, not a search tree. Is the preorder listing alone still enough to rebuild it?
